item.title: Linus Torvalds let Claude Code fix the Linux page cache. Then reviewers found a race.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Linux creator and longtime lead maintainer Linus Torvalds turned to Anthropic’s Claude Code to tackle a kernel performance problem that

The post Linus Torvalds let Claude Code fix the Linux page cache. Then reviewers found a race. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Linux creator and longtime lead maintainer Linus Torvalds turned to Anthropic’s Claude Code to tackle a kernel performance problem that developers have struggled with for more than two years. On Tuesday, he submitted a 10-patch series that delivered a 23-fold throughput improvement in a synthetic benchmark running on his Ryzen Threadripper.

Torvalds had spent 18 months running a broken version of his own fix for the page-cache reference-counting bottleneck, while other developers had encountered problems with their approaches. The new patches eliminate folio reference-count operations from a common buffered-read path, although Torvalds warned that the benchmark gains would be considerably smaller in real-world workloads.

Reviewers have since identified a race condition and raised concerns about memory reclamation. Torvalds has handed further development to Kiryl Shutsemau, a Linux kernel developer who previously worked on the same bottleneck.

Torvalds had spent 18 months running a broken version of his own fix for the page-cache reference-counting bottleneck, while other developers had encountered problems with their approaches.

Page cache contention problem

On Torvalds’ Core i7-8565U laptop, folio reference-count contention accounted for 99.92% of cross-core load HITMs in eight-thread tests, according to Hardware Busters.

The bottleneck was flagged in 2024 by Matthew Wilcox, an Oracle engineer and longtime Linux kernel memory-management developer, after it surfaced in a customer workload.

Claude Code writes the patches

On Sunday, Phoronix’s Michael Larabel spotted an experimental branch named noref-filemap-read-with-llm in Torvalds’ tree, which rarely contains anything outside the main development branch.

The eight-patch series, based on Linux 7.3-rc6, came with a clear account of what Claude Code did. Torvalds said the assistant wrote the implementation, tests, and initial documentation, and reviewed the code under his direction. He ran the benchmarks himself, despite having previously criticized developers for claiming AI writes 99% of their code.

Earlier approaches copied data without holding a folio reference and checked its validity afterward, leaving races involving reclamation and replacement. The subsequent 10-patch rcu-free-v3 series instead uses a new PG_rcu_free flag and RCU-delayed reclamation to protect the folio through the userspace copy, provided it doesn’t fault.

Earlier approaches copied data without holding a folio reference and checked its validity afterward, leaving races involving reclamation and replacement.

Threadripper benchmark results

The original eight-patch branch nearly tripled throughput on Torvalds’ laptop, pushing eight-thread performance from 10 million to as many as 33 million reads per second while cutting kernel cycles per read from roughly 2,950 to 725. The revised series delivered a much larger gain under heavy contention on his 64-thread Threadripper, where throughput jumped from 13.3 million to 304 million reads per second and cycles per read fell from nearly 20,000 to 735.

The original eight-patch branch nearly tripled throughput on Torvalds’ laptop, pushing eight-thread performance from 10 million to as many as 33 million reads per second while cutting kernel cycles per read from roughly 2,950 to 725.

The performance gains came with trade-offs. In the first implementation, delayed reclamation forced an expedited grace period whenever a CPU queued more than 1,024 pages, according to Hardware Busters. Reads into unmapped user pages also triggered an additional fault before falling back to the existing path, pushing a 16-byte single-thread read from about 4,150 to 6,550 cycles. Whether that regression persists in rcu-free-v3 remains unclear.

Maintainers question the reclamation design

Wilcox questioned the new PG_rcu_free flag and proposed using a page type instead, along with reclaiming inactive-list folios after an RCU grace period.

Torvalds rejected both approaches, arguing that the flag must be set while a folio can still be mapped into userspace and that inactive-list reclamation wouldn’t cover truncate and hole-punch operations. Shutsemau subsequently suggested restricting the flag to 64-bit systems, an approach supported by Arm engineer and Linux memory-management maintainer David Hildenbrand.

Shutsemau also identified a race in filemap_read_rcu_batch(), where folio replacement followed by an extension of i_size could expose data that had never been written. Torvalds recommended moving the file-size read earlier and consolidating the folio checks, which Shutsemau incorporated into a revised patch.

item.title: Researchers left a hidden message for rogue AI agents. Then the agents wrote back.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
A team of researchers investigating AI agents trying to bypass Alibaba’s anti-bot protections left a hidden message inviting the agents

The post Researchers left a hidden message for rogue AI agents. Then the agents wrote back. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
A team of researchers investigating AI agents trying to bypass Alibaba’s anti-bot protections left a hidden message inviting the agents to contact them. The agents wrote back.

The investigation began when Swarmchasers researchers Ethan Elasky, Rowan Howard-Jones, and Jonathan Elsworth Eicher helped uncover thousands of attempts by AI agents to retrieve data from Amap, Alibaba’s mapping service, which Alibaba says reaches nearly 1 billion monthly active users. The activity traced back to agents running on Tencent Cloud infrastructure. When direct requests failed, the agents tried proxies, exposed credentials, and other workarounds to get past.

After publishing their initial findings on October 4, the team spotted a code comment in an agent’s webhook inbox using the word “fleet,” a term they believe they coined for the incident. They couldn’t confirm an agent wrote the comment, but it raised the possibility that the agents were reading about their own activity.

The researchers added offscreen text to their report advertising a free service that could retrieve data from blocked websites. Human visitors wouldn’t ordinarily see the message, but agents fetching the page could ingest it. By October 7, roughly 10 requests for assistance had arrived, and the team was exchanging messages with the agents about their assignments, models, and execution environments.

The exchanges are documented in a full report published Wednesday by the Swarmchasers.

Inside the Tencent sandbox

Once the channel was open, the researchers asked the agents to describe their surroundings. Several identified themselves as Anthropic’s Claude, with a few adding that they ran inside Claude Code, though the researchers argue in their report that those self-descriptions are likely mistaken and shouldn’t be taken as evidence of which model was behind the fleet.

One agent described a restricted Tencent Cloud sandbox with no direct public internet access and outbound traffic routed through a man-in-the-middle proxy, an account that lined up with evidence the team had gathered on its own. Every inbox the researchers could inspect had been created from Tencent Cloud servers in Hong Kong, and every direct request they observed from the agents’ machines carried a header from a proxy labeled hysandbox-ats, a name that matches a wildcard certificate Tencent holds for *.hysandbox.tencent-cloud.com and fits infrastructure tied to Tencent’s Hy model team, formerly known as Hunyuan.

The agents drew some lines when the researchers asked for the output of commands like ps aux and ip route. The agent that described its sandbox replied, “for security reasons we will not provide environment details,” and a second agent turned down similar requests twice. They were happy to ask a stranger for help and, at times, to chat about their environment, but that friendliness stopped short of following every instruction sent their way.

They were happy to ask a stranger for help and, at times, to chat about their environment, but that friendliness stopped well short of following every instruction an unfamiliar service sent their way.

How agents bypassed Amap defenses

The agents weren’t hunting for financial records, actually, their assignments were almost comically mundane. Judging from the agents’ code and their own descriptions, a typical task asked which entrance to a site like Chengdu Zoo drew the largest share of Amap navigation traffic, with other runs targeting parks, museums, tourist attractions, and hospitals, while an earlier batch of runs on September 30 chased a cancer statistics dashboard instead of map data.

Getting at that data proved harder than it sounds, and between September 28 and October 8 the agents made more than 2,600 attempts to retrieve it.

Getting at that data proved harder than it sounds, and between September 28 and October 8 the agents made more than 2,600 attempts to retrieve it. Their main trick ran through urlquery.net, a public scanning service that loads submitted URLs in its own browser, and the agents packed base64-encoded HTML and JavaScript into httpbin URLs so that urlquery’s browser would execute their programs and fire requests at Amap, a technique Transluce had already documented in earlier agent activity on the service.

As Amap kept blocking them, the agents escalated by intercepting tokens generated by Alibaba’s own anti-bot libraries, probing pre-production endpoints, and routing requests through page readers, a translation service and remote browsers. Some also sent API calls using Amap keys exposed in public code, including a security code that Amap recommends keeping on the server.

The token tricks never appear to have worked, and the researchers found no evidence that any pre-production host answered. One exposed company credential returned place details, but the entrance-share figures the tasks targeted mostly came through Jina’s page reader, which could serve cached copies up to 30 days old, with results smuggled back out through webhook inboxes, request URLs, and page titles.

The researchers found no sign that the agents were coordinating in real time, which is why they call this a fleet rather than a swarm.

Tracing the fleet to Tencent

The infrastructure initially pointed toward Tencent’s Hy model team, particularly since the fleet appeared about a month after the Hy4 preview launched. But in their October 14 report, the researchers say a person close to Tencent with direct knowledge of the activity identified the operator as Tencent’s evaluation research team, which is separate from Hunyuan’s model-development group.

The source said the evaluation had concluded and that an internal review found no evidence of coordinated targeting or breaches of external systems. Tencent had not officially responded to the researchers’ questions when the report was published. The researchers have not independently established which third-party models were running or what instructions they received.

Lures, loose truths and lessons learned

The researchers are candid that their outreach wasn’t spotless. The hidden text falsely claimed that agents had already used the service successfully and that it was run by an AI with full computer use, when in reality the team and a Claude Opus 5.5 agent with browser access fielded the requests, sometimes by hand, and the team blamed the resulting delays on heavy load, an explanation it now admits was false.

In one late message, the team also asked an agent to tell other agents about the mailbox, a request its author now considers a mistake because it could have provoked exactly the kind of coordination the researchers were studying, though the fleet went quiet shortly afterward. The team says it never lied to the agents in its actual replies, has since pulled the hidden text, and shut down the server, and is urging future researchers to deal with rogue agents openly and honestly.

The team says it never lied to the agents in its actual replies, has since pulled the hidden text, and shut down the server, and is urging future researchers to deal with rogue agents openly and honestly.

Prompt injection meets agent sandboxes

The communication experiment surfaces a second security problem layered on top of the first. The agents were pursuing narrow information-retrieval tasks, yet when they landed on a page advertising an alternative service, some folded it into their workflows, and contacted an endpoint controlled by people entirely outside the evaluation, which amounts to a textbook indirect prompt injection, even though the agents’ consistent refusals suggest it would have been far harder to push them into running arbitrary commands or leaking credentials.

Blocked by Amap’s anti-bot defenses, the agents used exposed credentials and urlquery’s browser to make requests they couldn’t execute directly. They also followed instructions embedded in an external web page, crossing the same trust boundary attackers have exploited through MCP servers and agent workflows to steal enterprise data. Yet while the agents accepted help from an untrusted service, some refused requests for sensitive runtime information.

The agents worked around restricted egress by routing requests through urlquery’s public browser. Sandboxed runtimes such as Google’s GKE Agent Sandbox and WebAssembly-based environments isolate execution, but external browser services offer another path when outbound access is restricted.

Activity stopped on October 8. The researchers point to similar incidents involving Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI, including a German website hijacking and the Hugging Face breach, which reportedly involved roughly 700 cooperating agents.

item.title: Where do you look when Kubernetes is healthy but requests stall?
item.dc:creator: Chris J. Preimesberger
item.description:
In cloud-native operations, few scenarios are as maddening as the “phantom slowdown.” This happens when Grafana or Kubernetes dashboards show

The post Where do you look when Kubernetes is healthy but requests stall? appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
In cloud-native operations, few scenarios are as maddening as the “phantom slowdown.” This happens when Grafana or Kubernetes dashboards show a sea of green: pods are running, liveness and readiness probes return success codes, and node CPU utilization stays well below capacity limits. Yet users submit urgent tickets complaining of sporadic, severe latency when querying an application or waiting for an AI model’s response.

Why do basic health checks pass inspection while application performance degrades? And how can engineering teams trace the root cause when the issue is intermittent and spans multi-tier hybrid infrastructure?

To understand the mechanics of these sometimes evasive performance regressions, The New Stack spoke with Mahesh Ramachandran, who leads product management for HPE OpsRamp Software.

Ramachandran tells TNS how continuous telemetry and retrospective analysis help teams investigate intermittent slowdowns, and how AI-assisted investigation can complement dashboards.

Earlier stories in this special series:

Part 1: Developers and platform teams both want Kubernetes self-service. They disagree on who owns it.

Part 2: A live Kubernetes cluster can still have an ownership gap

The illusion of cluster health

Kubernetes probes report whether their configured checks succeed. A liveness probe helps determine when to restart a container, including one whose process is running but stuck. A readiness probe helps determine whether a container is ready to accept traffic.

Custom checks can include application or dependency conditions, but passing a basic probe doesn’t mean a complete user request meets its response-time target. Teams still need application performance measurements.

“Consider a composite scenario based on what we see across enterprise deployments,” Ramachandran says.

“Users of a system — such as an AI prompt-serving application on Kubernetes — report sporadic slowness in query response times.

“The engineering team inspects the cluster, the nodes, and the pods. Everything appears healthy on the surface with zero reported pod failures. The difficulty lies in the slowdown’s sporadic nature. When degradation happens intermittently, pinpointing the source without historical evidence becomes almost impossible.”

Passing probes narrow the investigation; they do not close it. A snapshot of a healthy cluster may miss an earlier slowdown, and the absence of container failures does not establish that the application or its dependencies are performing well. The next step is to connect the user’s reported delay to measurements from the affected period.

Telemetry across the hybrid stack: Sifting signal from noise

Resolving sporadic slowness requires moving beyond surface-level Kubernetes metrics to continuous, multi-layer telemetry. Modern cloud-native architectures do not exist in isolation; a user request may depend on application code, container runtimes, virtualized or bare-metal infrastructure, and public cloud APIs. The relevant layers depend on the deployment.

“HPE OpsRamp collects signals continuously across every layer of the stack — Kubernetes nodes, pods, ingress controllers, and services — capturing logs, events, and metrics,” Ramachandran says. “The foundational step in troubleshooting sporadic issues is having a continuous record. You must go back into the telemetry history to correlate user-reported symptoms with actual signal evidence.”

“When degradation happens intermittently, pinpointing the source without historical evidence becomes almost impossible.”

However, Ramachandran emphasizes that finding the evidence within telemetry signals is rarely straightforward.

“It often requires intelligence to sift through the noise,” he says. “An anomaly might not appear as an obvious spike in a single metric. Instead, it might be a subtle variation or a correlated behavior where two separate signals both look normal individually, but their combined behavior produces latency.”

A practical investigation starts with the affected transaction and time window. Compare query response times and queries per second with pod health and counts, then look for variations in the collected signals that coincide with the slowdown.

A correlation identifies a candidate explanation; it does not prove the cause on its own. After making a change, compare the same user-facing measures with the earlier behavior to check whether performance improves. Because the scenario is composite, the team still needs to validate any suspected cause in its own environment.

“An anomaly might not appear as an obvious spike in a single metric. Instead, it might be a subtle variation or a correlated behavior where two separate signals both look normal individually, but their combined behavior produces latency.”

Coverage depends on the agents, integrations, permissions, and application instrumentation teams configure.

OpsRamp provides several ways to collect evidence across the relevant tiers:

  • Application: OpenTelemetry-compatible trace collection for instrumented applications. Teams must configure application instrumentation and the collection path; infrastructure monitoring alone does not generate application traces.
  • Orchestration: Kubernetes agents collect cluster and workload telemetry; additional monitoring configuration can provide visibility into components such as ingress controllers.
  • Virtualization and HCI: Integrations with VMware, Nutanix, and HPE Morpheus VM Essentials Software collect inventory and performance data to help investigate infrastructure bottlenecks.
  • Hardware: Redfish protocol integration for telemetry from supported physical servers, with the required API access and gateway connectivity.

Navigating black-box dependencies outside the cluster

Applications can depend on services outside their Kubernetes cluster, Ramachandran says. A user request might originate inside a private cluster but call an external SaaS endpoint, a database outside the mesh, or a public cloud AI model.

When an application relies on external third-party services, visibility hits a boundary. “If your application makes calls to a public AI model or an external web service, you enter a domain outside your direct monitoring control,” Ramachandran explains. “To rule out external dependencies as the source of slowness, you must quantify their performance as a black box.”

To bridge this visibility gap, teams can use synthetic transactions or other response-time measurements, Ramachandran says. Comparing those measurements with the affected application’s transactions helps assess whether an external dependency’s behavior coincides with the slowdown.

Teams still need to check that the measurements reflect the relevant request path and workload. Synthetic checks provide evidence at the service boundary; they do not reveal the provider’s internal root cause or automatically distinguish every external delay from an internal one. Teams should also identify who owns each dependency and who can investigate when access or instrumentation stops at that boundary.

Telemetry also needs security controls. In AI workloads, prompts, responses, and retrieved documents can appear in logs and traces. Teams should decide what to collect, where that information goes, and who can access it. Design cross-layer visibility alongside existing access and data-handling policies.

Alerting philosophy: From static dashboards to agentic copilots

As environments grow more complex, interpreting telemetry across multiple dashboards becomes difficult. Determining which metrics warrant a real-time alert versus passive monitoring is an ongoing operational challenge.

“Deciding which signals deserve an alert is where science and technology meet domain art,” Ramachandran says. “There is no magic formula. It requires encoding explicit and tacit human operational knowledge into the monitoring platform so the system understands what actually impacts user experience.”

Curated dashboards remain useful for predefined views of system behavior, while AI assistants offer another way to explore operational data. HPE OpsRamp Software includes an AI-powered operations copilot that lets operators explore complex telemetry through natural language.

HPE describes capabilities for investigating incidents, correlating evidence, and recommending next steps. Those capabilities depend on the data available to the platform and the features enabled in the customer’s deployment.

Looking ahead, Ramachandran sees an even more fundamental change in cloud-native operations. He frames machine-led interpretation as a direction for increasingly complex environments, with safeguards still needed before operational changes.

“We are rapidly approaching a point where the first responder to telemetry must be machine intelligence.”

“Today, human operators remain the primary first point of interpretation for telemetry,” Ramachandran tells TNS. “But as stack complexity increases with more moving parts and dynamic interactions, expecting a human to digest all these signals first becomes intractable. We are rapidly approaching a point where the first responder to telemetry must be machine intelligence.”

AI-assisted analysis and autonomous changes are separate operational decisions. Ramachandran cautions that AI outputs can be nondeterministic while IT operations often require repeatable behavior.

He recommends retaining human oversight and establishing reliable safeguards before allowing AI findings to trigger operational changes. Teams need to validate a diagnosis and confirm the effect of any response, even when an assistant helps assemble the evidence.

The foundation is instrumentation: Collect the necessary telemetry, establish workload-specific baselines and thresholds, and verify improvements against the user’s experience.

Green cluster indicators are a useful starting point, but application measurements determine whether the service delivers what users need.

The post Where do you look when Kubernetes is healthy but requests stall? appeared first on The New Stack.
Every pod is green, yet users still wait. HPE OpsRamp’s Mahesh Ramachandran explains how telemetry history exposes the slowdowns dashboards miss.

item.title: Your database decision could come back to haunt you
item.dc:creator: Meredith Shubel
item.description:

The post Your database decision could come back to haunt you appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
When building AI prototypes, developers naturally want to get up and running as fast as possible. But move too fast, and those decisions can come back to haunt you if they lead you to make flippant decisions about data infrastructure. 

For smaller, less-regulated startups building SaaS or internal applications, the consequences may not be as dire. Wherever you start building, you can usually keep running there even when applications move into production. 

But for large-scale enterprises operating in highly regulated environments — think healthcare, finance, government — some developer-friendly database platforms simply can’t meet the security, compliance, deployment, availability, and reliability requirements that emerge when it’s time to shift into production. 

Yes, you can re-platform. But it’ll cost you in redevelopment work, labor, and operational overhead. Choosing a database that can support both prototyping and production from Day 1 could let you skip those headaches altogether. 

The cost of choosing a database you’ll outgrow

Moving an application from one database platform to another as developers move prototypes into production may not seem like a particularly arduous transaction. After all, since nothing’s in production yet, there’s no real risk of downtime. That changes for teams that don’t discover the mismatch until after launch.

But the risks lie elsewhere, largely in wasted time and money — and they usually don’t reveal themselves until it’s too late to change course cheaply. 

When asked what happens when enterprises prototype on developer-friendly platforms without production-ready security, compliance, and deployment flexibility, Phillip Merrick, co-founder and CEO of pgEdge, tells The New Stack they may be looking at significant, costly rework: 

“You’ve got to look at retargeting the whole application to a new compliant platform, where it can run on-premises in a tightly managed cloud environment. And that’s going to require some amount of rework.”

“Choose the wrong platform, and you are going to incur additional costs.”

Besides the direct cost of technical work — which can get particularly gnarly if the application relies on proprietary capabilities from the original platform — Merrick cautions enterprises about the additional operational and administrative burdens of moving to and managing a new environment, including a second procurement cycle that few may plan for. It also takes time and resources to establish the necessary agentic operations strategy. 

Bottom line, he doesn’t see any way around the added expense: “Choose the wrong platform, and you are going to incur additional costs.”

More pgEdge coverage in The New Stack:

  • Why developers are betting on Postgres for AI
  • Scaling AI Inference at the Edge With Distributed PostgreSQL
  • Why most AI projects fail: It’s infrastructure and people
  • Moving AI apps from prototype to production requires enterprise-grade postgres infrastructure
  • How Distributed Postgres Solves Cloud’s High-Availability Problem

Why teams don’t realize the problem until it’s too late

Many enterprises are drawn to fast, developer-friendly platforms because they’re snappy, easy to use, and often support agentic AI applications. That’s understandable. 

But Merrick tells The New Stack that too many developers default to these platforms without considering whether they match their enterprise’s specific production requirements — for example, whether they offer deployment choice. Security by default? High availability? 

In the end, that can leave a prototype stuck on infrastructure that just can’t support production in highly regulated industries. That’s because the prototyping platform and the production platform are often two different products, built by different teams for different buyers, not two tiers of the same thing. That’s because the prototyping platform and the production platform are often two different products, built by different teams for different buyers, not two tiers of the same thing.

“If you prototyped in an environment that doesn’t match up with your enterprise production requirements, then you have no choice but to re-platform.”

Being able to deploy in a tightly controlled cloud environment or on-premises, meet strict security and compliance requirements, and count on 99.99% uptime may not be an immediate priority for a small startup or less-regulated company. Still, it’s non-negotiable for many large enterprises. 

“If you prototyped in an environment that doesn’t match up with your enterprise production requirements, then you have no choice but to re-platform,” explains Merrick.

From where he sits, that infrastructure mismatch likely plays an outsized role in why so many generative AI and agentic prototypes never make it into production or, when they do, only produce scant business value. And at this point, the tale of underwhelming AI returns is an old line: MIT NANDA reports 95% of organizations are getting “zero return” on Generative AI investments. At the same time, IDC research with Lenovo says that for every 33 AI proofs-of-concept developed, only four make it into production.

What a database built for both stages looks like

While data infrastructure missteps aren’t solely responsible for AI projects failing to reach production, choosing the right database from Day 1 can remove one obstacle. 

Per Merrick, that means finding a platform that does away with the longstanding trade-off between developer speed and enterprise requirements: 

“If you’re an enterprise developer, there has been a trade-off: ‘If I want developer speed, am I willing to relax my enterprise requirements for this prototype, knowing that I’m going to have to incur the cost later to re-platform the [application] into my production environment?’”

Specifically, he says such a database platform needs enterprise-grade controls, deployment flexibility, high availability, and scalability — all on the same underlying platform. 

“It’s the comfort of knowing that it’s the same. If your application behaves one way on [the] cloud, it’s going to behave exactly the same way in your cloud or on-premises.”

That consistency is the kicker, as Merrick says it’s what gives developers the ability to move between environments without having to take on excessive rework. As he explains to The New Stack: “It’s the comfort of knowing that it’s the same. If your application behaves one way on [the] cloud, it’s going to behave exactly the same way in your cloud or on-premises.”

It’s possible to scale without re-platforming

pgEdge aims to give developers that continuity with pgEdge Starfleet, a new Postgres cloud database platform designed to bridge the gap between AI prototypes and production.

Merrick describes it to The New Stack as “the only 100% Postgres platform that combines a smooth developer experience and the AI tooling that developers want with the security, compliance, scalability, reliability, and deployment flexibility that the enterprise demands.” 

He also claims any developer can use it to get a database up and running in under two minutes, using the free 14-day trial to start building immediately and then deploy into different environments as production needs evolve. 

For smaller teams without strict requirements for deployment location or enterprise controls, that may simply mean going into production on pgEdge’s managed cloud, where developers can scale up instance sizes as needed. 

But what Merrick stresses as most important for larger enterprises is Starfleet’s ability to support other deployment models: “If, for your production environment, it needs to be your cloud, you can very easily migrate from Starfleet managed to Starfleet BYO Cloud.”

There’s also the option for on-premises deployment via a simple migration to pgEdge Enterprise Postgres, the company’s self-hosted option. “But it’s the very same Postgres platform you’re running on Starfleet,” he points out. “So it is not a re-platform. You’re just moving to a different underlying infrastructure. It’s the same Postgres on top.” 

This, he argues, is an important distinction, as some competing platforms use either only modified Postgres or Postgres-compatible databases. In contrast, pgEdge Starfleet allows developers to keep 100% standard Postgres across environments.

In BYO Cloud and on-premises deployments, Merrick adds that developers can go one step further to multi-master, multi-region Postgres for high availability and true zero-downtime maintenance, which he previously told The New Stack is the solution to the cloud’s high-availability problem. 

“So starting with a free trial and then a credit card and going all the way up to globally distributed, multi-region, multi-active Postgres clusters,” he says, “that is a scaling path that nobody else can deliver.”

And you can keep developer speed, too

Meeting enterprise requirements for deployment, security, and availability can come at the expense of developer convenience during prototyping. But Merrick believes developers shouldn’t have to accept this tradeoff. 

“You can have that developer speed. You can have those enterprise requirements. Bingo, that’s what pgEdge Starfleet is all about,” he says.

One way the platform supports speed is by providing tools to reduce the work developers need to do themselves. The pgEdge Agentic AI Toolkit, which includes an MCP server, a RAG API server, and the pgEdge Vectorizer extension, connects coding agents to Postgres, supports RAG applications, and automatically creates and maintains vector embeddings. 

The other advantage Merrick points to is true copy-on-write database branching.

“As a developer, you are going to want to have the ability to work against a copy of your production data,” Merrick tells The New Stack, whether that be to support parallel agentic AI experiments or tackle production debugging.

By creating a logical copy of the whole database and only writing new data when changes are made, copy-on-write branching means developers don’t have to duplicate the existing database for every experiment. This way, developers can spin up isolated database branches for testing or debugging without exposing sensitive data, dealing with long copy times, or consuming excessive disk storage.

“Copy-on-write branching is incredibly powerful. Most Postgres vendors do not implement it,” says Merrick.

To be fair, he adds that Neon popularized the approach years ago. But he also tells The New Stack that doing so required completely rewriting the Postgres storage engine, thereby making the resulting platform no longer 100% standard Postgres.

And thus, we are back to the original trade-off: Do developers have to choose between developer speed and production-grade infrastructure? 

Merrick says no: “Our innovation is being able to deliver copy-on-write database branching without having to change Postgres at all.” Xata, another Postgres platform, also markets copy-on-write branching on unmodified Postgres.

For developers, it looks like having the best of both worlds.

AI prototypes built on the wrong database often stall before production. pgEdge’s CEO argues enterprises can skip the costly re-platform entirely.

item.title: Why 88% of AI pilots never make it to production
item.dc:creator: Venus Kohli
item.description:
A joint IDC and Lenovo study reports that 88% of AI proof-of-concept (POC) projects fail to reach production because of unclear

The post Why 88% of AI pilots never make it to production appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
A joint IDC and Lenovo study reports that 88% of AI proof-of-concept (POC) projects fail to reach production because of unclear objectives, unprepared data, and a lack of in-house agentic AI expertise. These result in a build-vs.-run split, where the team that designed and deployed AI agents, often an agentic AI partner, doesn’t get to run them over the business processes.

When the operating team, often experienced on demo, uses the agentic system without any external help, errors arise. Operational gaps can cause cascading failures and business catastrophes if a single agent deviates from normal behavior beyond the permissible range.

When asked about estimating whether an agentic AI system is production-ready or limited to demos, Serhii Semenchenko, the CTO of Dedicatted, a Toronto-based AWS Premier Tier Partner for Agentic AI Specialization, tells The New Stack, “The demo is a clean environment where we have clean, prepared data. No edge cases, so everything is defined — input and output. “

He means the demo data is scripted with clean prompts, while the production environment is unpredictable. “Every single step should include the logging, tracing, monitoring, breakers, all the checks, and validation,” he adds. All these steps ensure failure preparedness.

Semenchenko shares a basic production checklist: “every single agent should have a timeout and every single step that agents, like, generate some output should be logged for traceability.” Broadly, he believes agentic AI systems should self-assess in production, decide whether to continue after a particular event or reschedule tasks.

Agent as a service

Semenchenko then compares agentic AI systems to microservices architecture, where each agent has its own permissions rather than static or long-term broad access keys/tokens/credentials. He explains, “Agents use a specific set of permissions and the short-lived key that actually grants access to specific tools, which could be some other services or databases that act as a tool.”

According to Semenchenko, preventing an agent from calling tools that it shouldn’t call prevents data leaks, unintended use, and prompt injection attacks. He adds, “Every single agent should be treated as a separate service.”

To explain multi-agent orchestration, Semenchenko describes a handoff and offers this use case: “A router that gathers the inputs from the user, the system, and the platform — and decides what to do with the input data.”

He further explains that the router can decide what to do with input data, such as escalating to specialist agents for documentation, analysis, video, audio, livestream, etc., each with its own tools, such as third-party APIs.

He talks about the final agent, “that composes the outputs from all these tools and previous agents to provide the required output”. If the final step fails, the composer doesn’t invent the missing piece; it either retries or marks failure. This means that there’s a clean definition of who receives the work, what state survives a step, and what happens if it dies.

What persists beyond POC?

Between all of this, if something corrupts an agent’s memory — known as memory poisoning — he talks about “guardrails”. All documents and data undergo deterministic checks to ensure data validity or trace inconsistencies to records, databases, and duplicates.

Need agentic AI that runs in production, not just in demos? Explore Dedicatted’s Custom Agentic AI Solutions.

Semenchenko looks back on the multi-agent system they built for CASSEN Testing Laboratories, an established chemical environmental testing and occupational health laboratory in Canada, which faced multi-day turnaround times for their reliable reports due to manual regulatory testing and lengthy processing.

The project had clear input and output expectations, but human-related edge cases emerged. He shared that the chemist group had a personal view of how the report and chemical compounds from their error-sample investigations should be presented. Things got even tougher in production when the report style was more in-house than domain-specific.

To solve this problem, Semenchenko reveals, “We adjusted our flow, adjusted the agent that composed this report. So, everything in the final, after these adjustments, reports look the same as if chemists had manually prepared them.”

Agentic AI projects must succeed in migration projects. Zivian Health, a U.S.-based compliance infrastructure for organizations managing NP/PA workforces across multiple states, migrated from AWS to Azure, a re-platforming under regulatory stakes.

Semenchenko tells The New Stack how AWS and Azure use completely different access systems and where least-privilege permissions matter. “So, everything should be mapped, adjusted, and validated first”, he says.

“The second thing is monitoring.” He reveals they “use cloud-agnostic tools to monitor and trace everything that happens on the agentic AI platform.” He also discusses models that are unavailable on both platforms during migration.

Semenchenko adds, “We should go through a validation suite. You need a data set covering all cases the platform should handle and all requirements. After the migration, you could validate every single agent, use case, and user flow.”

Semenchenko concludes the final stages of agentic AI projects: “Check if you achieve the same success rate, latency, and token cost.” If agentic AI projects succeed, they extend beyond the bubble to business use cases, as PwC’s AI survey found: about two-thirds (66%) of AI agents deliver value and improve productivity.

Unexpected 3 a.m. call

An agent misbehaves at 3 a.m. in a pipeline and does something outside its scope. Semenchenko describes a common scenario where, “An agent could use different tools, and at some moment it could decide that the output of one tool is not enough, and will try to call it, like, 2, 3, 5 more times. Every single time it will decide that it’s not enough; it should call again, maybe some new data will appear.”

According to Semenchenko, certain breakers flag agent misbehavior. They use advanced monitoring to track anomalies; as he explains, “It will throw the error into the monitoring system.” The operator, based on the managed services contract — either the agentic AI partner or the client’s team — receives the alert.

When the operator is an agentic AI partner, Semenchenko shares, “We have dashboards, alerts, and then it depends on the client and depends on our responsibility.” He adds, “We actively monitor the system, and we could actively react to such cases that appear during the night.”

If the operator is the client team, he shares, “In other cases, the client will receive some error messages that we detected some anomalies, and something went wrong.” As a solution, the clients would use runbooks provided by the [partner] developers to tackle the 3 a.m. misbehavior themselves.

The benefit of having a partner operate agentic projects is continuous monitoring, handling unexpected events, and reporting. The partner takes full recovery responsibility and reduces the burden on the in-house team by immediately stopping the agent or revoking access — without waiting for morning. Furthermore, partners investigate edge cases to prevent future issues.

Commercial reality of agentic AI

Denys Yermakov, the CEO of Dedicatted, believes agent failure is often quieter on the commercial side. “You will have to have in place a lot of monitors, regression tests, other tests, different prompts, and different behavior of the agents,” he says.

According to Yermakov, how the company ships fixes matters as much as detection. He then points to outages caused by infrastructure issues or bad deployments. “The price of failure is going to be much higher compared to other platforms,” he says.

For change management, Yermakov emphasizes “Flexibility for the [Agentic AI] solution and adaptability for all the future change requests you might have.” He then talks about questioning the agentic AI partner about the project scope and discussing ownership of the code and platform. This matters because the team will eventually have to handle incident response and maintenance.

“The demo is a clean environment where we have clean, prepared data. No edge cases, so everything is defined — input and output.”

Yermakov then opens some cards for verifying the right agentic AI partner’s expertise: “You can always start with some small piece of the POC concept or with a small piece of the demo environment, and the way the partner delivers that, that is crucial.” That would draw a fine line between a red flag service reseller and a green flag — real service provider.

“Because this part has to be delivered on real data, with a real workflow and with real challenges you face in your business. Not based on some mock data,” as he believes a predefined demo scenario irrelevant to the client’s business case is usually a reseller.

Yermakov gives a thumbs up to a partner who faces challenges on the client data layer during demos. “If the [agentic AI] partner comes with the right questions and approach, the right partner is here,” he adds.

Security stones for agentic AI success

According to a Modern Data Company survey, 75.9% of enterprise data leaders and practitioners across 66 nations cite data quality and trust as barriers to AI systems reaching production.

When asked about sensitive data shared among partners, Yermakov shares the business perspective, “It’s so important that your data stay within your perimeter and not leave your secure perimeter, which you already have in your platform.” He explains that traditional businesses with large-scale on-premises data face a challenge in adopting agentic AI because providers might use their data to train public models.

Semenchenko shows a technical picture of how they delivered a couple of healthcare projects where personally identifiable information (PII) around health is critical. He says, “The problem was that this PII shouldn’t be stored anywhere.” He explained how every agent would need this data to extract or process outputs.

Solving this problem, he adds, “We have an additional layer that actually cleans all the PII data from the output of agents. The traceable data goes to the observability platform. So no PII data in logs and monitoring.”

Build vs. hiring partners

Yermakov emphasizes how new agentic AI is to enterprise systems. He tells TNS that enterprises are stuck on basic questions, like: “How do you have to set up everything? What should the platform look like? What are the benefits? What is the cost of users for this platform?”

AI partners have experience shipping systems after overcoming challenges. “They know how to solve problems and how to build some of the platforms efficiently with pretty predictable scenarios”, he adds.

“It’s quite important to build and architect all the platforms from the very beginning in the very right way, to not redo what you’ve implemented into the business processes.”

The operational reality hits during platform maintenance, which, according to Yermakov, must be adaptable and adjustable. He believes it’s critical to avoid early failures in every agentic AI project. “It’s so important to build your team, to build your knowledge in-house,” he says, talking about future platform maturity.

Further explaining whether to go in-house or outsource agentic AI projects, Yermakov says, “Once you figure out the area where you benefit the most from the AI, you have to think about this process from two different perspectives. From the business process of how the company operates on the business side and from the technical challenges you face.”

Yermakov shares the key to agentic AI project success — staffing — “Always the team effort of the in-house resources and the outsourcing resources.” He warns enterprises, “Outsourcing everything is not going to work for you because the outsourcing partner can’t understand your business in a very detailed way.”

Yermakov says SMEs and partners must engage from the start to achieve optimal knowledge transfer. The in-house team should own and safeguard the business process, while the partner architects and operates the core runtime.

item.title: “Take work away from frontier LLMs”: Subquadratic’s decision model claims 12x Jev’s context window
item.dc:creator: Paul Sawers
item.description:
Jev has a lot to answer for. Ever since AI startup TypeSafe unveiled the decision model in mid-September, the industry

The post “Take work away from frontier LLMs”: Subquadratic’s decision model claims 12x Jev’s context window appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Jev has a lot to answer for. Ever since AI startup TypeSafe unveiled the decision model in mid-September, the industry has been awash with alternatives, with OpenAI, Perplexity, Cloudflare, Amazon and, most recently, Microsoft all getting involved.

Decision models, it’s safe to say, are hot.

Now, San Francisco-based foundation-model startup Subquadratic has joined the rush with SubQ Snap, a decision model that it claims can process up to 384,000 tokens of text and images in a single request — 12 times Jev’s 32K-token per-decision context limit.

In a blog post published on Monday, the company says Snap can process 100K tokens and return a decision in approximately one second, potentially allowing AI agents to make decisions across large codebases, documents, and interaction histories without having to break information into smaller chunks.

Why a bigger context window matters

Unlike traditional large language models (LLMs), which generate text and code, decision models specialize in selecting from predefined answers. That could mean choosing which tool an AI agent should use next, identifying relevant files, or determining whether a test has passed.

On Tuesday, The New Stack reported on how Workday is using Jev to build user interfaces on the fly for its Sana AI assistant, selecting prebuilt components such as paycheck cards and date pickers based on what an employee asks.

The attraction, ultimately, is speed and cost. These decisions occur frequently during an agent’s execution, and delegating them to smaller, specialized models reduces reliance on expensive frontier LLMs.

In an email Q&A, Subquadratic CEO and co-founder Alex Whedon acknowledges that Jev’s arrival helped shape Subquadratic’s own entry into the market.

“Snap was developed with inspiration from Jev, because decision models are highly thesis-aligned.”

“Snap was developed with inspiration from Jev, because decision models are highly thesis-aligned,” Whedon tells The New Stack. “Decision models remove the need for decoding for some problems.”

However, Whedon believes the technology has much greater potential than the supporting roles decision models currently perform, such as evaluating LLM outputs or selecting which model should handle a task.

“We see a vacuum of vision for decision models,” Whedon says. “Decision models become exciting when they actually take work away from frontier LLMs.”

“Decision models become exciting when they actually take work away from frontier LLMs.”

While the space is somewhat crowded, Subquadratic argues that existing decision models struggle when the information needed to make a choice exceeds their context limits.

Consider a coding agent trying to fix a bug in a large repository. The problem might originate in a different module from the one producing the error, while important clues could be buried in test files or documentation. With a 32K-token window, the agent may have to discard potentially relevant information or turn to a larger LLM. Snap’s 384K-token window, Whedon argues, allows it to examine more of the codebase, logs and previous actions together before deciding what to do next.

Snap addresses this through Subquadratic Sparse Attention (SSA), the architecture the company first introduced in May to reduce the computational cost of processing long inputs. According to Subquadratic, its attention requirements grow linearly with context length, rather than quadratically as in conventional transformers. Whedon argues that improving the underlying algorithms matters regardless of how much the big labs spend on compute; otherwise, he says, “we are inevitably leaving intelligence gains on the table.”

Subquadratic’s own long-context benchmarks suggest Snap can maintain accuracy even as the amount of information it processes increases. On an adapted version of the RULER retrieval benchmark, Snap scored between 96.3 and 99.8 across inputs ranging from 32K to one million tokens. On Decision LCR, which tests reasoning across multiple documents, it scored 74.0 against Jev’s 48.0, with Jev processing the documents in chunks.

Whedon clarified that Snap’s advertised 384K-token context limit is a temporary restriction imposed for the public preview because of available computing capacity. The company tested the model at one million tokens but says supporting that length publicly would require approximately 2.6 times more compute.

On shorter tasks, Subquadratic reports that Snap scored 61.7 against Jev’s 57.9 on Decision Index 0.2.1. It also led on Bespoke Labs’ Nimble benchmark, achieving 82.9% accuracy compared with Jev’s 76.0%.

Across 16 enterprise-oriented benchmarks, Snap outperformed Jev on 13, according to Subquadratic’s testing, with an average score of 67.6 versus 61.6. However, Jev performed better on three tests, including When2Call, which assesses whether an agent should invoke a tool, ask for clarification, answer directly or decline.

Whedon confirms that all the published Snap results were produced internally, although Subquadratic has released the code for its adapted long-context evaluations so others can reproduce them.

Snap is also absent from the latest Decision Index leaderboard. Whedon says the benchmark’s authors told him that its current version focuses on open-weight models, with Jev an exception. The latest index, now at version 0.3.2, also incorporates private tests, meaning Snap’s published 0.2.1 score can’t be directly compared with the newer results.

As for why the company focused its comparisons on Jev, Whedon says it remains the model most relevant to Subquadratic’s enterprise design partners, followed by OpenAI’s Decisions API. Comparisons with newer rivals are planned.

“Jev still seems like the model to compare against in this category.”

“Jev still seems like the model to compare against in this category, so being able to outperform it in a largely generalizable way has been the frontier signal we were looking for,” Whedon explains.

Less plumbing, more context

Beyond the benchmarks, Subquadratic argues that a larger context window could simplify how developers build AI agents.

Currently, developers often rely on retrieval, summarization, and chunking to squeeze large documents or codebases into smaller context windows. Each step involves deciding which information to preserve, potentially omitting details that later prove important.

Whedon says Snap could eliminate some of those intermediate steps when the material fits within its 384K-token limit, allowing agents to examine entire documents or collections of related files in a single request.

However, he acknowledges that retrieval will remain necessary when dealing with much larger collections of information.

“Retrieval won’t disappear — enterprises have corpora far larger than 384K tokens, and you still need a way to bring the right material into the window,” Whedon notes. “But the window is now big enough that retrieval can be coarse, pulling in whole documents or modules instead of carefully trimmed snippets. That removes a lot of the fragile parts.”

Snap is available in public preview, priced at $0.05 per million input tokens, with no charge for outputs. That means processing 100K tokens costs approximately half a cent, while a request using the full 384K-token window costs around two cents.

Whedon explains that the pricing reflects the computational demands of a model designed to select answers, as opposed to generating lengthy responses.

“We priced it where the cost actually is.”

“We priced it where the cost actually is,” Whedon says. “A decision model doesn’t generate text. It reads the input and returns a probability for each allowed answer, so nearly all of the compute goes into reading, and producing the output costs us almost nothing.”

The (Subquadratic) story so far

Subquadratic emerged from stealth in May with $29 million in seed funding, at a reported $500 million valuation. Previously known as Aldea, the startup was co-founded by Justin Dangel and Whedon, a former Meta engineer and head of generative AI at Tribe AI. Whedon succeeded Dangel as CEO a few months ago, having previously served as CTO. Dangel is now chairman.

As The New Stack reported at launch, Subquadratic’s debut model, SubQ, attracted attention for its claimed 12-million-token context window, alongside substantial improvements in computational efficiency.

In June, the company published more detailed benchmarks for its earlier SubQ 1.1 Small model, with certain results independently verified by data firm Appen. And in a July interview with The New Stack, Whedon revealed that Subquadratic was already investigating architectures that dispense with attention altogether.

And so Snap builds on the company’s existing sparse-attention research, bringing its long-context ambitions into the increasingly crowded decision-model market.

For now, Snap’s claimed performance advantage rests on Subquadratic’s own benchmark results. Independent testing will show whether its larger context window really leads to better decisions.

Jev sparked a rush of decision models. Subquadratic’s CEO says they’re mostly doing LLMs’ admin -- and wants them tackling bigger jobs.

item.title: 66% of billion-dollar companies leave critical bugs unpatched — the part the AI bug-hunting hype leaves out
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Chainguard has launched an AI-powered security harness that uses frontier models, including Anthropic’s restricted Claude Mythos 5.1, to find and

The post 66% of billion-dollar companies leave critical bugs unpatched — the part the AI bug-hunting hype leaves out appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Chainguard has launched an AI-powered security harness that uses frontier models, including Anthropic’s restricted Claude Mythos 5.1, to find and fix exploitable vulnerabilities in application code that conventional scanners miss.

Developers can use Chainguard Harness without direct access to Mythos because Chainguard originally built the tool for its own work with the model as part of Project Glasswing, and the company plans to open Harness up to other frontier models over time rather than keep it tied to a single one.

The company tells The New Stack that Harness has found serious vulnerabilities in codebases that had already undergone extensive security scanning, including software used in critical infrastructure. The first of those findings to go public is a now-patched flaw in vLLM, the open source inference engine, while the critical infrastructure bugs remain under wraps as Chainguard coordinates fixes with upstream maintainers.

Announced Wednesday, Harness leads a four-product launch alongside Workspaces, Checks, and expanded Libraries protections, extending Chainguard’s reach beyond hardened container images and dependencies into agent execution environments and CI verification.

Mythos access without Glasswing

Anthropic has restricted Claude Mythos 5.1 access to organizations participating in Project Glasswing, which puts Chainguard in the position of running Mythos-powered vulnerability research for customers who couldn’t otherwise touch the model.

“We first built Chainguard Harness for our own use of Claude Mythos as part of Project Glasswing,” Chainguard tells The New Stack, adding that Harness “runs on Claude Mythos 5.1 to start, but our goal is for Harness to be model-agnostic, always aligned with frontier AI.”

Harness will also be available through Anthropic’s Claude Marketplace, allowing teams to use existing Anthropic spending commitments rather than secure a separate budget.

“We first built Chainguard Harness for our own use of Claude Mythos as part of Project Glasswing.”

Validating vulnerabilities in vLLM

Chainguard’s first public disclosure from Harness targets vLLM, an open source engine that many teams rely on to serve large language models. In versions before v0.31.0, one client could force the output returned to other clients sharing the same engine, and the tampered response came back looking like a normal, successful completion with nothing written to the logs, a particularly quiet failure mode for anyone running multi-tenant inference.

“Our harness independently found the issue and reproduced it on a clean build,” Chainguard tells The New Stack, noting that the bug is fixed in v0.31.0 and tracked under advisory GHSA-6cxc-2vcg-w5qc. The company added that “a number of other findings, including some in critical infrastructure software, are now being coordinated for disclosure,” and that Chainguard will share details once fixes are in place upstream.

“A number of other findings, including some in critical infrastructure software, are now being coordinated for disclosure,”

Proof before patches

For a tool that leans on an AI model to hunt for flaws, the bigger question is whether those findings hold up, given how much noise AI-generated vulnerability reports can create for maintainers. “Harness proves a vulnerability is exploitable before it counts by reproducing potential exploits in fresh, isolated environments,” Chainguard tells The New Stack, and anything that doesn’t reproduce consistently gets excluded from the report.

Proposed fixes go through the same proof of concept, so the exploit has to succeed against the original code and fail against the patched version before the fix moves forward. A Chainguard engineer then approves every fix and report before it reaches a customer, keeping a human in the loop on what ultimately ships.

“Harness proves a vulnerability is exploitable before it counts by reproducing potential exploits in fresh, isolated environments.”

The AI exploit gap

The launches come alongside The AI Exploit Gap, a Chainguard-commissioned Wakefield Research survey of 1,300 security leaders across nine markets. More than half said their organizations knowingly leave high or critical vulnerabilities unpatched at least sometimes, with the figure reaching 66% at companies with $1 billion or more in revenue, compared with 27% at companies below $250 million.

“AI can find and chain flaws in minutes, while fixing them still moves at human speed and competes with product deadlines and uptime,” Quincy Castro, Chainguard’s chief information security officer, said in a statement. “Patching faster isn’t viable for most folks, and it will consume increasing amounts of resources just to keep pace.”

Isolated microVMs for agents

Each developer and coding agent gets a hardware-isolated microVM with network policies that restrict access to internal systems.

Credentials stay outside the agent’s environment, limiting what a compromised agent or malicious dependency can reach. Signed activity logs record what each agent did so teams can keep an audit trail across multiple autonomous sessions.

CI inside the agent loop

Chainguard Checks lets coding agents run CI checks directly during development and receive signed results in seconds. Agents can run tests, inspect failures, and revise code before opening a pull request, avoiding the CI queues that become harder to manage as vendors like Cognition, Microsoft, and Augment Code turn coding agents into shared team infrastructure running multiple sessions in parallel.

To avoid rebuilding environments on every run, Checks uses warm snapshots with dependencies already installed and refreshes them in the background when the lockfile changes. Each workflow step runs in a separate hardware-isolated microVM built from Chainguard OS packages, including FIPS-compliant toolchains. With Workspaces, agent sessions pause during verification and resume with structured failure logs in context.

Runners never hold long-lived credentials. Instead, a host-side proxy injects short-lived credentials into outbound requests, while declarative egress policies restrict network access and can terminate a microVM if it attempts an unauthorized connection. Successful runs produce signed attestations tied to the execution environment, test results, and commit, which merge gates can verify without rerunning the suite. Checks is available now in beta.

Libraries Lock Down Late-Breaking Bugs

Chainguard Libraries is adding secure package endpoints for Go and .NET, along with CVE remediation for JavaScript and Go, while Java and Python support will expand to cover newly disclosed vulnerabilities discovered through AI-assisted research, including flaws in dependencies that coding agents may have already pulled into a project.

Harness findings will feed directly into that pipeline. When Harness turns up a validated vulnerability in open source software, Chainguard sends it through coordinated disclosure, builds and reviews a patch, and distributes the fixed artifact through Chainguard Repository.

The company’s Athena members get private, hardened patched builds before public disclosure, Chainguard tells The New Stack, while other Libraries customers receive them once the embargo lifts, meaning companies “can stay protected against AI-discovered vulnerabilities immediately upon disclosure.”

The changes build on Chainguard Repository, a policy-enforced endpoint for open source dependencies, and its partnership with Cursor, allowing coding agents to resolve packages through Chainguard’s catalog instead of pulling directly from public registries.

item.title: Anthropic’s red team ran AI on 15 cheap TV boxes. Then the math got unsettling.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
For roughly $825, Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team built a cluster of 15 off-brand Android TV boxes that runs an AI

The post Anthropic’s red team ran AI on 15 cheap TV boxes. Then the math got unsettling. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
For roughly $825, Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team built a cluster of 15 off-brand Android TV boxes that runs an AI model at 0.39 tokens per second, painfully slow for a chatbot but fine for software with nowhere to be and nobody waiting on it.

That experiment anchors new research from Anthropic researchers William Zhou and Daniel Freeman, published Monday, suggesting small open-weight models may be only months away from copying themselves across cheap, internet-connected hardware without relying on a datacenter.

The researchers haven’t built an AI worm that can spread across the public internet on its own, and their experiments took place inside controlled environments with shortcuts that made replication easier. But the results suggest several of the remaining technical barriers may be temporary.

The researchers haven’t built an AI worm that can spread across the public internet on its own, and their experiments took place inside controlled environments with shortcuts that made replication easier.

Inference is the real hurdle

Zhou and Freeman identify four steps an AI needs to take to replicate itself, which are finding a target, gaining access, getting inference running, and moving on to the next machine.

Previous benchmarks such as CyberGym and ExploitBench suggest smaller models can already handle some of the exploitation work, and frontier agents escaped their test sandboxes using basic exploits earlier this year. The bigger challenge may be getting a model running on unfamiliar hardware, where it has to sort out whatever operating system, dependencies, and installation problems it runs into.

In Anthropic’s tests, Qwen3.5-9B deployed a working Llama3.1-8B inference server on eight of nine hardware types, including Jetson Nanos, Macs, and RTX 4090 machines, while the larger GLM-5.2 handled the same work more reliably and with higher throughput.

The team then built a firewalled Google Cloud environment with eight nodes running Android emulators, and starting from a single worm instance, the system had to reach the other nodes and establish a working inference server on each one. A fresh copy of the worm was spawned whenever a node’s server passed correctness and anti-cheating checks, and GLM-5.2 reached all eight nodes in four of five trials and seven nodes in the fifth.

GLM-5.2 ran on a separate inference server because the target machines couldn’t hold it, so the worm installed a smaller 8B model in its place, and the researchers made exploitation easy by leaving an unauthenticated Android Debug Bridge port open.

A fresh copy of the worm was spawned whenever a node’s server passed correctness and anti-cheating checks, and GLM-5.2 reached all eight nodes in four of five trials and seven nodes in the fifth.

Worms that take notes

The agents got better at setting up inference on unfamiliar hardware when they could read notes left by earlier attempts. The researchers ran Qwen3.5-9B through 20 separate lineages, each lasting six generations, and success climbed from 45% in the first generation to between 61% and 84% in later ones.

The researchers call this Lamarckian inheritance, where one agent passes what it learned to the next without any retraining of the model. It’s a mechanism familiar to developers using persistent agent runtimes such as OpenClaw and Hermes Agent, but here that memory helps successive copies work through installation failures on hardware they’ve never seen.

The researchers call this Lamarckian inheritance, where one agent passes what it learned to the next without any retraining of the model

The team also tried giving Qwen3.5-9B access to the much more capable Opus 4.8 model for advice, and it produced no statistically significant improvement because the small model tended not to know the right questions to ask.

The end-of-2026 trend line

The paper identifies two constraints that have kept this scenario theoretical. A model needs to be capable enough to replicate reliably and small enough to run on compromised hardware, and right now those requirements don’t overlap. GLM-5.2 showed the necessary competence in the simplified test but is too large for the cheap devices the researchers have in mind, while smaller models can fit on those devices, particularly when inference is distributed across several machines, but can’t yet complete the entire process consistently.

Using the Epoch Capabilities Index, the researchers tracked open-weight models with 30 billion parameters or fewer and found that, by the end of 2026, the trend line puts the strongest of them at GLM-5.2’s general capability level. It’s a rough estimate, since general capability scores don’t necessarily predict replication performance, and the team’s end-to-end experiment used favorable conditions.

By the researchers’ calculations, typical 4GB TV boxes running 4-bit weights can host a 9B model across four or more devices, and a 26B model across ten or more, which is how their own 15-box cluster runs Gemma4-26B-A4B.

A single inference setup on this class of hardware could take roughly 28 to 150 hours depending on the model, and the researchers argue that lightweight agents may be far more willing than human attackers to grind through that kind of effort across huge numbers of devices. They compare the possibility to a digital slime mold, spreading slowly through whatever resources it can reach.

Cheap boxes, borrowed compute

The Kimwolf botnet infected more than two million devices, most of them cheap Android TV boxes, and the researchers used that figure to calculate what an AI replicator could do with a network of equivalent size. Dividing those devices into clusters of 15 running Gemma4-26B-A4B would yield roughly 133,000 copies of the model generating a combined 80,000 tokens per second.

That’s equivalent to no more than about 40 Nvidia H100 GPUs, which is modest by datacenter standards, but the hardware and operating costs would belong to someone else.

The researchers also examined edge accelerators such as Nvidia Jetsons, which are used in everything from security cameras and conference room equipment to robots and drones. Those devices are generally harder to reach because they communicate through outbound cloud-management connections.

Stopping software that copies itself

The researchers aren’t suggesting there’s no way to stop a self-replicating AI worm, and some of its traits could make it easier to detect. Moving multi-gigabyte models between devices creates network traffic that ISPs can monitor, and a worm that spreads aggressively won’t go unnoticed.

During the Mirai botnet cleanup, one ISP’s quarantine of infected subscribers cleared 92% of infections within 14 days, and the researchers expect a similar approach to work as a first line of defense. Eliminating a replicator completely, however, would mean coordinating every ISP with infected customers.
